sermon:
## The Beginning You Cannot Skip
*Why every shortcut to wisdom ends in the same ditch*

**Text:** Proverbs 1:1-7; 2:1-15 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 9:10; Job 28:28; Psalm 111:10; 1 Corinthians 1:18-25

We live as if wisdom were information we have not gotten around to downloading yet. As if the difference between the life we have and the life we wanted were a matter of better advice, the right podcast, one more book on the shelf. Proverbs walks into that assumption and shuts it down in a single line.

Not a tip. A threshold.

**Wisdom has a door, and the door has a name**

The book opens by telling you what it is for, "To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight" (Proverbs 1:2). It promises prudence to the simple, knowledge to the young, more learning to the wise. It sounds like a curriculum. And then, before you can sign up, it names the only entrance: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction" (Proverbs 1:7). Not the reward of knowledge. The beginning of it. The threshold you cross before the first real thing can be learned.

The Hebrew word is *yirah*, fear. Not the cringing terror of a slave waiting for the lash, and not the watered-down "respect" we reach for to make the verse comfortable. It is the reverence of a creature standing in front of the Creator and knowing the difference. It is the trembling of someone who has seen who God is and who he himself is and stopped pretending the two are close. Psalm 111:10 says the same thing the same way: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Job 28:28 says it after thirty-seven chapters of suffering that taught him nothing he wanted to know: "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." Three witnesses, one verdict. The door is not open at the top of the climb. It is the first step, and there is no climbing without it.

**The competence that is folly underneath**

Here is what unsettles me about this, and it should unsettle you. Proverbs is not contrasting the wise man with the obvious fool, the drunk, the loud, the reckless. It is contrasting the wise man with the competent man who never bowed. Chapter 2 promises that if you cry out for insight, "then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:5), and the very next breath warns about men of "crooked" paths who are "devious in their ways" (Proverbs 2:15). These are not incompetents. They are skilled. They are effective. They get what they want. And the book calls them fools, because every skill they have is bent around a self that never knelt.

This is the part that exposes the church as much as the world. We have built a Christianity that is fluent in competence and shy about fear. We have leadership conferences and almost no trembling. We can run the organization, manage the brand, exegete the verse, and never once stand undone before the holiness of God. I have done this from a pulpit. I have prepared the sermon with skill and walked into the room with no fear of the LORD in me at all, and I called the skill wisdom. It was folly dressed in competence. It is the most respectable folly there is, because it produces results, and results are the disguise.

The simple man in Proverbs is not stupid. He is unanchored. He knows things and fears nothing, and so the things he knows have no center to organize them. He is a library with no librarian. Knowledge without the fear of the LORD is not neutral information waiting for a use. It is power handed to a self that will bend it toward itself every time.

Chapter 2 makes the same point from the other side, and it is worth slowing down on. The wisdom it promises is not handed over for asking nicely. "If you receive my words and treasure up my commandments... if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:1-5). If, if, if, and then. The wisdom is real and it is available, but it is dug for, the way you dig for buried silver, not stumbled onto by a person strolling through life with no fear in him. And the reason the digging matters is named two verses later: "the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding" (Proverbs 2:6). Wisdom is not a skill you generate. It is a gift God speaks, and you cannot receive a gift from a God you do not fear enough to come to with open hands.

**The wisdom of God, on its knees at a cross**

We distrust this because we want wisdom we can possess on our own terms, wisdom that flatters us as we acquire it. And here Proverbs and the gospel say the same hard thing. Paul wrote that "the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing," that God chose "what is foolish in the world to shame the wise," that Christ "became to us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:18, 27, 30). The wisdom of God did not come as a better strategy. It came as a crucified man. It came as the place where every human competence is bankrupted and a kneeling creature receives what he could never earn.

Which means the fear of the LORD is not a phase you pass through on the way to maturity. It is the posture maturity never leaves. The most learned saint in the room is the one most undone by the holiness in front of him. The cross does not graduate you out of the fear of the LORD. It teaches you what that fear costs, and Who paid it.

You cannot skip the beginning and arrive at the end. There is no advanced wisdom that left the door behind. The door is the trembling, and the trembling is the start of everything you actually wanted to know.

Wisdom starts on its knees.

## Two Women Calling From the Street
*The voice you answer is the life you build*

**Text:** Proverbs 8:1-36; 9:1-18 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 1:20-21; John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17; 1 Corinthians 1:24

There are two voices on your street, and they are both calling your name. Not your secret name. Your common one, the name everyone uses, the one that means ordinary, unremarkable, on your way to somewhere with your guard down. Proverbs says wisdom and folly both stand "at the highest places in the town" (Proverbs 9:3, 14) and call to the same passersby. Same corner. Same crowd. Two voices.

You are answering one of them right now.

**Wisdom cries aloud, and she was there before the world was**

Wisdom does not whisper from a hidden grove for the initiated. "Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand" (Proverbs 8:1-2). She stands where the roads meet, where you actually live, where the decision gets made before you knew it was a decision. And then she tells you who she is, and the room should go quiet. "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth" (Proverbs 8:22-23). She was there "when he established the heavens," "when he marked out the foundations of the earth," and she was "beside him, like a master workman," "daily his delight, rejoicing before him always" (Proverbs 8:27-30).

This is not a clever saying about good decisions. This is wisdom as something woven into the structure of reality before there was a reality to structure. The same wisdom that laid the foundations of the earth is the voice on your corner. To answer her is to come into alignment with the grain of the universe. To refuse her is to run against it and call the splinters bad luck.

And notice what she promises, because it is not what folly promises. "I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me" (Proverbs 8:17). "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35-36). That last line is the whole book in a sentence. To refuse wisdom is not a neutral preference for a different lifestyle, it is, in her own words, to love death. The choice on the corner is not between two flavors. It is between life and self-injury, and the terrible thing is that the one injuring himself thinks he is simply choosing what he likes.

**Folly sets the same table, and she counts on the dark**

Here is what should stop you. Folly is not crude. Proverbs 9 gives wisdom and folly identical scripts. Wisdom "has built her house," "slaughtered her beasts," "mixed her wine," "set her table," and calls, "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed" (Proverbs 9:1-5). And folly, "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", sits at her door and calls, in the very same words, to the very same people: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here" (Proverbs 9:13, 16). The invitation sounds the same. The corner is the same. The only difference is what is served and where the guests end up. "He does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:18).

That is the whole danger. Folly does not announce itself as death. It announces itself as a meal. It uses wisdom's vocabulary, come, eat, satisfy the hunger you actually have. It is not the absence of an invitation. It is a counterfeit of the true one, pitched to the same appetite, banking on you not asking what is in the cup. The wine looks the same in the glass. The table is set with the same care. And one of them is laid in a tomb.

We imagine the fool as someone who chose evil over good with his eyes open. Proverbs says no. The fool is someone who answered a warm voice on his own street that offered him exactly what he was hungry for, and never asked who was cooking. I have answered that voice. I have justified the turn into folly's door with reasons that sounded like wisdom in my own mouth, because folly always speaks in wisdom's accent. The choice is not loud. It is daily, ordinary, and dressed like dinner.

**The Wisdom who built a house and called us in**

Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is personified, present at creation, the master workman, daily delight. John opens his gospel in the same key: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God... All things were made through him" (John 1:1, 3). Paul says of Christ that "by him all things were created," that "in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16-17), and that Christ is "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). The voice on the street has a face now. The master workman who delighted before the foundation of the earth is the carpenter who set a table in an upper room and said, take, eat.

So the daily choice is not finally between two abstractions. It is between two persons calling from the same corner of your ordinary life. One built a house and gave his body for the feast. One sets a table over a grave and counts on you not looking down. They call in the same words. They are not serving the same meal.

And this is where I have to stop pointing at the simple young man and turn the mirror. I have answered folly's voice in full daylight and told myself it was wisdom, because she had learned to talk like the truth. I have called the turn into her door discernment, or freedom, or just being honest with myself, and never once asked who set that table or where its other guests had ended up. The fool in Proverbs is not a stranger I have been describing. He has worn my face on more ordinary afternoons than I want to count.

You will eat at one of these tables today. You are choosing which one in things too small to notice.

Two tables. One life. Choose.

## The Power of an Inch of Flesh
*Why your words are never as small as they feel*

**Text:** Proverbs 10:18-21; 12:18; 15:1-4; 18:21 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 16:24; James 3:5-10; Ephesians 4:29; Matthew 12:36-37

We have a theory that words are weightless. We deploy it constantly, "I was just saying," "I didn't mean anything by it," "they're only words." It is one of the most useful lies we tell, because it lets us do damage and claim we did nothing. Proverbs does not let the lie stand.

Proverbs weighs the tongue and finds it heavier than we can carry.

**Death and life are in an inch of flesh**

The verdict is stated without hedging: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21). Not influence. Not impact. Death and life, the two largest words the Bible owns, placed in the smallest member of the body. The same book draws the picture twice over. "There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing" (Proverbs 12:18). A sword thrust. Not a scratch, not a barb, a thrust, the kind that goes in to the hilt and does not come back out clean. "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1), and a few lines on, "A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit" (Proverbs 15:4).

Breaks the spirit. What that claims is enormous. Proverbs says a tongue can break a person at the level where they hold themselves together, not bruise the feelings, break the spirit. We have all had it done to us. We can name the sentence, years later, word for word, said by someone who has long forgotten saying it. They were just talking. We are still bleeding.

And the wound goes the other direction too, which is the part we forget. The same chapter that warns about the harsh word praises the healing one in the same breath. "A gentle tongue is a tree of life" (Proverbs 15:4), a tree of life, the image from the garden, planted now in the middle of an ordinary conversation by an ordinary person who chose the kind word. "The lips of the wise spread knowledge" (Proverbs 15:7). The tongue that can deal death can also be, for the person across the table, the nearest thing to Eden they will touch all week. Proverbs will not let us treat speech as small in either direction. The thing that can break a spirit can also be a tree of life, and we are handing one or the other across the table every day.

**Restraint is not weakness. It is love with a hand over its mouth.**

Then Proverbs does something we do not expect. It does not just warn against bad words; it praises the words you never say. "When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent" (Proverbs 10:19). The fountain of speech runs, and the longer it runs the more sewage comes up with the water, that is the plain mechanism Proverbs names. "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many" (Proverbs 10:20-21). The righteous tongue feeds. The fool's tongue floods.

We treat restraint as a failure of nerve, the thing you do when you are too timid to say the brave thing. Proverbs treats restraint as a craft. The wise person is not the one with no opinion. He is the one who has felt the sword-thrust answer rise in his chest, recognized it for what it was, and chosen the soft answer that turns away the wrath instead. "Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body" (Proverbs 16:24). That is not the absence of speech. It is speech disciplined into an act of love. The wise person could wound and does not. That withheld blow is one of the quietest, costliest things a person ever does for another.

**The tongue no one can tame, and the Word who tamed himself**

And here is where I stop preaching at you and stand in it. James picked up Proverbs and made it worse. "The tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things" (James 3:5). "No human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:8-9). The same mouth. The same Sunday. I have stood at a pulpit and blessed God with the tongue, and used the same tongue in the parking lot to diminish someone made in his image, and felt no contradiction in the moment. The poison does not feel like poison going out. It feels like honesty, or humor, or just saying it.

No human being can tame the tongue, which means the tongue is not a behavior problem. It is a heart problem with an exit. Jesus said it plainly: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34), and "on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak" (Matthew 12:36). Every careless one. The ones we were "just saying."

The only mouth that ever passed that judgment belonged to the Word made flesh, the one of whom it was said, "no deceit was found in his mouth." He bore the sword-thrust words of the mob and answered with silence and with mercy. The cross is, among everything else, the place where God absorbed every careless word we will ever account for. So Paul can turn it forward: "Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up... that it may give grace to those who hear" (Ephesians 4:29). Grace to those who hear. Your tongue can carry the very thing the cross carried to you.

Death and life are in it. You are handing one of the two to someone today, in a sentence you will forget by dinner and they will keep for years.

Your words are never neutral.

## The Gospel According to the Sluggard
*The most self-deceived man in the book*

**Text:** Proverbs 6:6-11; 24:30-34; 26:13-16 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 13:4; 20:4; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12; Colossians 3:23

We think of laziness as a small sin, a soft one, the kind you confess with a smile. The sluggard is the comic relief of the book. And that is exactly the disguise Proverbs is tearing off. The sluggard is not funny. He is the most self-deceived man in Proverbs, and his disease is the one most likely to be ours, because it never feels like sin while you are doing it.

It feels like rest. It feels reasonable. It is the slow ruin of a life, one excuse at a time.

**Go to the ant, and notice who has no ruler over him**

Proverbs does not lecture the sluggard. It sends him outside to look at a bug. "Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest" (Proverbs 6:6-8). The ant has no manager. No one checks her work. No one wakes her. And she labors anyway, because the work is in her, not over her. That is the whole indictment of the sluggard hiding in a sentence about an insect. The sluggard does nothing unless he is made to, and there is no one to make him, so he does nothing, and calls it freedom.

Then the warning lands with a strange image. "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man" (Proverbs 6:10-11). Not a process. An ambush. He thinks he is choosing rest in manageable increments, a little, a little, a little, and what he is actually doing is leaving the door open for a man with a weapon. Poverty does not creep in this picture. It kicks the door. The ruin he was avoiding by inches arrives all at once.

**The vineyard, the wall, and the sleep that costs everything**

Proverbs gives us the sluggard's estate as a parable in chapter 24, and it is one of the most haunting things in the book. "I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down" (Proverbs 24:30-31). The teacher walks past, and "I looked and received instruction" (Proverbs 24:32). He learns wisdom not from a lecture but from a ruin. The wall is down. The protection is gone. The harvest is choked. And the man who owns it did not torch it or sell it. He slept it away, "a little sleep, a little slumber", the identical phrase, returned like a refrain, because the mechanism never changes.

There is one more turn of the knife in chapter 24, and it is the line that exposes the sluggard's real problem. After the teacher walks past the ruined vineyard, he names the cause: "a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man" (Proverbs 24:33-34). It is the very same sentence from chapter 6, repeated word for word, because Proverbs wants you to see that the man's ruin was not a single dramatic failure. It was a refrain. It was the same small choice, made the same small way, on a thousand ordinary mornings, until the wall fell. No one decides to ruin a vineyard. He decides to sleep in, a little, again, and the thorns do the rest.

Then chapter 26 shows you what it is like to actually live with this man, and it stops being abstract. "The sluggard says, 'There is a lion in the road. There is a lion in the streets'" (Proverbs 26:13). He has a reason. He always has a reason, and it is always almost plausible. "As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed" (Proverbs 26:14), motion without going anywhere, the hinge that swings all day and never leaves the frame. And the killing line: "The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly" (Proverbs 26:16). There it is. He is not just lazy. He is convinced he is the only one who sees clearly. Everyone else is naive about the lion. The self-deception is the disease, and the laziness is only the symptom.

**The Lord who labored, and the death that came like a robber**

This is where I have to climb inside the indictment, because the sophisticated version of the sluggard wears my clothes. I have called avoidance discernment. I have called procrastination prayer, "I'm waiting on the Lord" over a thing the Lord told me to do six weeks ago. I have built a wall of plausible reasons around a vineyard going to thorns and felt wiser than the seven men telling me to get up. The sluggard is not the man on the couch. He is the man with a reason for the couch that sounds like wisdom in his own ears.

Proverbs is blunt: "The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied" (Proverbs 13:4). Paul was blunter: "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But this is not finally a sermon about productivity, and Proverbs is not a self-help manual for hustle. The diligence it commands is the fruit of the fear of the LORD reaching down into a Tuesday. "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23). The Lord himself was no sluggard, he said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working" (John 5:17), and he worked the work the Father gave him to the last word: "It is finished." The diligence Proverbs wants is not anxious self-justification. It is the calm faithfulness of a person who knows his labor has an Owner, and that the Owner finished the only work that saves.

The robber is real. The wall comes down by inches and falls all at once. And the most dangerous version of you is not the one who knows he is failing, it is the one with a reason that sounds like rest.

Poverty arrives like an armed man.

## What Your Money Knows About Your Heart
*The most honest thing in your house*

**Text:** Proverbs 3:9-10; 11:24-28; 22:1-9; 30:7-9 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 19:17; Matthew 6:21; 2 Corinthians 9:6-8; 1 Timothy 6:17-19

There is a witness in your house that does not lie. It does not care what you said in the small group, or what you posted, or how you would describe your priorities if someone asked. It keeps a perfect record of what you actually love, and it is available for audit at any time. It is your bank statement. Proverbs knew this long before there were statements to read.

Money is not just a resource. It is a revealer.

**Honor him with the first, not the leftover**

Proverbs opens this with a command that reorders the whole thing. "Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty" (Proverbs 3:9-10). Notice the word, firstfruits. Not the tip left after the meal. The first. The portion that comes off the top before you have seen whether there will be enough, which is precisely the point, because giving the first is an act of trust and giving the leftover is an act of bookkeeping. What you do with the first dollar tells the truth about who you think is holding the rest.

And Proverbs immediately complicates the comfortable arithmetic we want to make of it. "One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want" (Proverbs 11:24). That is not a formula you can run for profit. It is a description of a world built by a generous God, where the clenched fist withers and the open hand is filled, not always with money, but always with life. "Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered" (Proverbs 11:25). "Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf" (Proverbs 11:28). The man trusting his riches and the man trusting his God can have identical balances. The difference is invisible on the statement and total in the soul.

**The good name, the poor man, and the lender you did not expect**

Chapter 22 widens the lens. "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold" (Proverbs 22:1). And then it tells you who is watching what you do with what you have: "The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all" (Proverbs 22:2). Your money is never a transaction between you and your stuff. There is a third party at the table, and he made both the rich man and the poor man you are deciding whether to see. "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9).

Proverbs says something almost scandalous about the poor man you might walk past. "Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed" (Proverbs 19:17). Lends to the LORD. The God who owns everything condescends to put himself in the position of your debtor when you give to someone who can never repay you. That is what your money knows that your mouth might not admit, whether you actually believe that, or whether you believe the poor are an interruption of your budget.

**The prayer of a man who feared both fortunes**

Agur's prayer is one of the most honest sentences a person has ever prayed about money, and it exposes both ditches at once. "Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, 'Who is the LORD?' or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God" (Proverbs 30:7-9). He is not afraid only of being poor. He is afraid of being rich, because he knows what wealth does to faith, it makes God seem optional. "Who is the LORD?" is the prayer of a full man who no longer feels his need. Agur knew his own heart well enough to fear his own prosperity.

I know that fear, and I do not pray it often enough. I have asked God for more and almost never asked him to protect me from what more would do to me. I have read "give me neither poverty nor riches" and quietly hoped he would ignore the second half. Because the danger of money is not that it is evil. It is that it works, it really does cushion, secure, comfort, and a comfort that works is the easiest god to serve, because it asks for nothing and delivers daily.

Jesus said it with no escape hatch: "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). Not where your heart is, your treasure follows, the other direction. The treasure leads. Move the money and the heart goes after it. Which is why generosity is not the tax you pay on a Christian life; it is the surgery that moves the heart toward God by moving the treasure first. And the gospel underneath it all is this: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). The one who owned everything gave the first and the all, kept back no leftover, and bought you with a generosity that cost him his life. We give because we were given to like that.

Pull your statement. It is testifying right now, whether or not you call it to the stand. And the question it answers is not how much you have but whom you trust, the LORD who gives, or the wealth that perishes the moment you lean your weight on it. Proverbs already told you which one stands: "the righteous will flourish like a green leaf" (Proverbs 11:28), and the leaf is green because it is rooted in something other than itself.

Honor God with your first.

## The Bed and the Whole of You
*Why Proverbs spends three chapters on one warning*

**Text:** Proverbs 5:1-23; 6:20-35; 7:1-27 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 9:17; 1 Corinthians 6:18-20; Hebrews 13:4; Song of Solomon 5:1

There are sins Proverbs mentions once and moves on. This one it circles back to three times, in three full chapters, with rising urgency and the same ending every time, a body, a grave, a life that did not have to end this way. When a wise book repeats itself like that, it is not moralizing. It is pleading. It has watched this happen to people it loved.

This is not a private matter. It is the protection of your whole life.

**Honey on the lips, wormwood at the end**

Chapter 5 will not let you pretend the danger is unattractive. "The lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword" (Proverbs 5:3-4). Proverbs grants the sweetness. It does not insult your intelligence by telling you the temptation is ugly, it tells you the temptation is honey, and then it tells you the bill. "Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol" (Proverbs 5:5). The honey is real. So is the wormwood. The lie is that you can have the first without the second.

And then chapter 5 turns from warning to something tender and almost shocking in its directness, it does not just say "don't," it says "drink." "Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well... Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth... be intoxicated always in her love" (Proverbs 5:15, 18-19). The remedy for stolen water is not no water. It is your own well, enjoyed without shame, on purpose, for a lifetime. Proverbs is not anti-pleasure. It is for pleasure so much that it refuses to watch you trade the deep, durable kind for a counterfeit that empties you out. "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Proverbs 9:17), folly's whole pitch in one line. The secrecy is the flavor. And the secrecy is the trap.

**The fire you carry in your lap**

Chapter 6 strips away the fantasy that this can be contained. "Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched?" (Proverbs 6:27-28). It is not a question. It is the law of the thing. There is no managed version of this fire, no careful handling that lets you hold it and stay unburned. And the cost is named without euphemism: "He who commits adultery lacks sense; he destroys himself who does it. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away" (Proverbs 6:32-33). Destroys himself. Not loses a season, destroys the self. The wound is to the man who does it, before it is anything to anyone else.

Then chapter 7 does the cruelest, kindest thing in the book. It makes you watch it happen. The father looks out his window and sees "a young man lacking sense" walking toward her house "in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness" (Proverbs 7:7-9). He is not dragged. He strolls. She comes out "dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart" (Proverbs 7:10), and her argument is brilliant, religious, even: "I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows" (Proverbs 7:14). She makes the betrayal sound like a blessing. "With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him" (Proverbs 7:21). And then the camera pulls back and the father tells you what you just watched: "All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter... He does not know that it will cost him his life" (Proverbs 7:22-23). He does not know. That is the horror. He thinks he is going to a meal. He is going to a killing floor, and he is walking there himself, in no particular hurry.

**The God who joined himself to a body, and to you**

I cannot preach this from above it. I am a man with a body and an imagination and a phone, and the twilight road in Proverbs 7 is paved now and lit by a screen and runs through every house including mine. The wisdom that says "can a man carry fire in his lap" is not naive about how strong the pull is. It is precisely realistic about it. It knows the honey is real. It loves you too much to let you sip it.

And here Proverbs and the gospel say something the world cannot say. Paul wrote, "Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body" (1 Corinthians 6:18). Then the reason, "do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you... You are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Bought with a price. The body Proverbs is fighting to protect is a body the Son of God took on himself, redeemed at the cross, and now indwells. Your faithfulness in the dark is not a rule you keep. It is a temple you guard, because someone bled to make it his.

So "let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled" (Hebrews 13:4) is not Puritan suspicion of joy. It is the same God who wrote Song of Solomon, "eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love" (Song of Solomon 5:1), telling you where the deep well actually is. The honey on folly's lips runs out into wormwood. The well in your own house is meant to be blessed, for a lifetime, without a grave at the end of it.

Drink from your own well.

## The Friend Who Wounds
*Why the kiss can lie and the wound can love*

**Text:** Proverbs 17:17; 18:24; 27:5-6, 9-10, 17 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 28:23; John 15:13-15; Galatians 2:11-14; James 5:19-20

We are starving for friendship and we keep mistaking flattery for it. We collect people who agree with us and call it community. We surround ourselves with voices that tell us we are right and feel loved, when what we have actually built is a room with no edges, a circle of soft mouths that will let us walk off a cliff smiling. Proverbs has no patience for it.

Proverbs says the friend you need is the one willing to hurt you.

**The brother born for adversity, the friend who sticks**

First Proverbs raises the bar on what the word even means. "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Proverbs 17:17). At all times, not in the good season, not while it is easy and mutual and fun, but at all times, including the time when loving you costs something and returns nothing. The brother is "born for adversity," made for the hard hour, the one who shows up precisely when everyone with lighter ties has found a reason to be elsewhere. And then a line that quietly exposes how thin our networks are: "A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother" (Proverbs 18:24). Many companions can be the very thing that ruins you, breadth bought at the cost of depth, a crowd that will not tell you the truth because no one in it is close enough to risk it.

We have confused being surrounded with being known. They are not the same thing. You can have five hundred companions and not one friend who will tell you that you are wrong, and Proverbs calls that condition not richness but danger.

**Open rebuke, faithful wounds, deceitful kisses**

Then comes the line that should reorder how you choose the people closest to you. "Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy" (Proverbs 27:5-6). Read it slowly. The friend wounds, and the wounds are called faithful. The enemy kisses, and the kisses are called profuse, abundant, generous, everything that looks like affection. The enemy will affirm you all the way down. The friend will cut you to keep you alive. The kiss can be a lie. The wound can be the truest love in the room.

We have it backwards because the kiss feels better in the moment and the wound feels like betrayal. So we drift toward the kissers and we resent the wounders, and we end up protected from everyone except the one thing that was going to destroy us. "Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel" (Proverbs 27:9). The sweetness, not the flattery, the earnest counsel. The hard word, well-aimed by someone who loves you, is itself a pleasure to the soul, the way medicine is to a man who finally wants to be well. "Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue" (Proverbs 28:23). Afterward. Not in the moment, afterward, when the wound has done its healing work and the flatterer's kiss has worn off into nothing.

And the mechanism, the most quoted line in the book on this: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Iron does not sharpen iron gently. It is friction, pressure, sparks, contact hard enough to grind. There is no sharpening at a comfortable distance. The blade gets honed by something that resists it, and a friendship with no resistance in it does not sharpen anyone, it only agrees, and dulls, and lets you go to ruin with your edges intact and useless.

**The friend who laid down his life, and the wound that saved us**

I have to confess where I sit in this, because it is not flattering. I would rather be liked than be faithful. I have softened the wound a friend needed because I did not want to spend the closeness it would cost. I have taken the kiss when I knew the kiss was a lie, because the wound was going to require something of me. And I have, more times than I will say, surrounded myself with companions instead of letting anyone close enough to sharpen me, because sharpening hurts and I am a coward about the right kind of pain.

The gospel gives this its center. Jesus said, "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends... No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends" (John 15:13, 15). He is the friend who sticks closer than a brother, the brother born for the worst adversity there is, ours. And he is the friend who wounds in faithfulness, the one who told Peter the truth he did not want, who said the hard thing at the cost of the crowd, who would not flatter a single person into a comfortable lie about themselves. Paul did the same to Peter to his face when Peter was wrong (Galatians 2:11), a faithful wound between brothers, recorded forever so the church would know what love looks like when it costs.

The deepest wound of all was his own. He was wounded, "pierced for our transgressions", and that faithful wound is the love that saved us. The friend who would not flatter us into hell took the wound that should have been ours. So when James says, "whoever brings back a sinner... will save his soul from death" (James 5:20), he is describing the highest act of friendship there is: loving someone enough to risk the relationship to keep the person.

Count the voices around you. The ones who will wound you are worth more than all the ones who only kiss.

Faithful wounds. Deceitful kisses.

## The City of the Heart and Its Walls
*Why ruling your spirit is the harder conquest*

**Text:** Proverbs 4:23; 14:29-30; 15:18; 16:32; 29:11, 22 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 25:28; Ephesians 4:26-27; James 1:19-20; Galatians 5:22-23

We admire the wrong strength. We are impressed by the person who detonates, who says the unfiltered thing, who "doesn't hold back," who lets it fly and calls it honesty and authenticity and being real. We have decided that the explosion is power and the restraint is weakness. Proverbs walks into that and calls it exactly backwards.

The one who conquers a city is weaker than the one who can rule his own temper.

**Guard the heart, because everything flows from it**

Proverbs hands you the central command before it gets to anger, and the command frames everything. "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life" (Proverbs 4:23). The heart in Proverbs is not the seat of feelings, it is the command center, the inner city out of which everything else proceeds. Guard it, the verse says, the way a city guards its walls, because what flows from it determines the whole of your life downstream. And then a few proverbs later it tells you what a broken-walled heart looks like in practice: it leaks anger.

The diagnosis comes in pairs of opposites, each one weighing the patient and slow against the hot and fast. "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Proverbs 14:29). "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger", we met that in the chapter on the tongue, and here is its companion, "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention" (Proverbs 15:18). And the line that ought to hang on the wall of every leader, every parent, every spouse: "A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression" (Proverbs 29:22). The angry man does not just sin; he *causes* sin, much transgression, a wake of damage in other people that he set in motion and will blame on them.

**The fool vents. The wise rules. And the wall is down.**

Proverbs draws the contrast between the fool and the wise man right at the point of the explosion. "A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back" (Proverbs 29:11). Full vent. We have made that a virtue and given it nicer names, processing, expressing, getting it out. Proverbs calls it the mark of a fool, because the fool's spirit has no governor on it, no wall, nothing between the impulse and the world. The wise man feels the same heat. He quietly holds it back. The feeling is not the failure; the venting is.

And then the image that should rearrange your whole idea of strength. "A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls" (Proverbs 25:28). Picture it. A city with its walls breached is not strong because nothing is contained, it is defenseless. Anyone can walk in. Anything can be taken. The man who cannot govern his temper looks formidable in the moment of the explosion, and he is in fact the most exposed person in the room, a city anyone can sack, because anyone with the right provocation owns the gate. The person who can make you lose your temper controls you. The wall is down, and everyone has noticed but you.

Which brings the book's verdict on what real strength is. "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). The conqueror takes a city, and Proverbs says the man who rules his own spirit has done the harder, greater thing. The outer conquest is easier than the inner one. We give medals for the city and shrug at the self-government, and we have it precisely reversed. "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Proverbs 14:30), even the body keeps the score of an ungoverned heart.

**The God who is slow to anger, and the wall he became**

I preach this as a man who has breached his own walls and called it righteous. I have raised my voice at my sons and labeled it conviction. I have let strife fly out of a hot heart and named it standing for truth, when it was just a city with no walls letting anyone who provoked me walk straight through the gate. The frightening thing James says is the thing I most need: "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:20). My anger has almost never been about God's glory and almost always been about my own, my will crossed, my comfort threatened, my kingdom slighted. I dressed the rot of my bones in the language of zeal.

Proverbs is not asking for a personality. The slow-to-anger man is not the man with no fire. He is the man whose fire is governed, and that governing is not white-knuckle suppression, it is fruit. "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience... self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). It grows. And it grows from one root: the character of the God who is, in his own self-description, "slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love." The wall around the city of the heart is finally a Person. Christ, provoked beyond anything we have known, mocked, struck, betrayed, crucified, ruled his spirit perfectly, and "when he was reviled, he did not revile in return." The only man who never breached his walls let his own body be breached for us, so that the Spirit who rebuilds the walls of the heart could come and dwell inside the city.

Paul, who knew anger was not always sin, gave the wall its gate and its curfew: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil" (Ephesians 4:26-27). The wall has a gate that opens for righteous anger and a curfew that closes it before the heart rots. That is rule, not repression.

The explosion you admire is a wall coming down. The restraint you overlook is the harder conquest in the world.

The fool vents. The wise rules.

## A Woman of Valor
*Wisdom with her sleeves rolled up*

**Text:** Proverbs 31:10-31 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 1:7; 8:1-3; 9:10; 1 Corinthians 1:30

The book ends where you do not expect a book of wisdom to end. Not with a maxim, not with a final principle, but with a portrait, a woman at work in an ordinary house, doing ordinary things, before dawn and after dark. After nine chapters of personified Wisdom calling from the heights, the book closes by showing you what she looks like when she gets a body and a household and a Tuesday to fill.

Wisdom, it turns out, has dirt under her fingernails.

**Not an impossible standard, but valor in an apron**

We have done damage to this passage by turning it into a checklist that crushes women under an impossible ideal. Read it as the writer wrote it and it is something else entirely. The opening word is the key the church usually misses: "An excellent wife, who can find?" (Proverbs 31:10). The Hebrew behind "excellent" is *chayil*, the word for valor, for strength, for an army. It is the word used of mighty warriors. This is not a woman defined by her decoration. She is a woman of *valor*, and the chapter that follows is not a beauty contest but a battlefield report.

And look where the valor lives, entirely in the ordinary. "She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands" (Proverbs 31:13). "She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household" (Proverbs 31:15). "She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard" (Proverbs 31:16). "She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night" (Proverbs 31:18). This is wisdom embodied in labor, buying, planting, trading, rising in the dark, working past it. Not a single mystical thing in the list. Wool. Flax. A field. A lamp burning late. The wisdom that was present at the foundation of the world (Proverbs 8) shows up at the end of the book as a woman buying a field and keeping her lamp lit, and Proverbs calls that valor.

**She opens her hand, and she opens her mouth**

The portrait does not stay inside her own walls. "She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy" (Proverbs 31:20). Everything the book has said about money and generosity, here it is with a face, the open hand, the same open hand Proverbs commended in the chapter on wealth, now belonging to a specific woman reaching toward specific need. And then the line that gathers up the whole book and gives it to her: "She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue" (Proverbs 31:26). Everything chapter 10 through 18 said about the tongue, death and life, the sword and the healing, and she has chosen the healing. Wisdom on her mouth. Kindness as her teaching. She is the tongue of the wise that feeds many, made flesh.

And Proverbs is careful to tell you the order of things, because we always get the order wrong. "Charm is deceptive, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). There it is. The book has come all the way home. It began with the verdict, "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7), and it ends with the same fear, now not as a principle stated but as a life lived all the way to the end. Everything in between, every proverb about the tongue and the money and the bed and the temper, was always meant to land *here*: in a person whose whole ordinary existence is organized around the fear of the LORD. The frame of the book is the fear of the LORD at both ends, and everything else is held inside it.

**The wisdom of God, who took a body and rose before dawn**

I have to be honest about how the church has used this woman, because I have used her this way myself. I have held this chapter over women as a burden, be all of this, do all of this, never rest, when the text is doing the opposite. It is not laying a weight on anyone. It is painting wisdom as a praise song. "Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates" (Proverbs 31:31). She is not being measured. She is being honored. The chapter is the household standing up to bless her, not a standard standing over her to condemn.

And it points past her. Personified Wisdom in Proverbs 8, present at creation, the master workman, the LORD's daily delight, finds her fulfillment not in a woman but in Christ, who "became to us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30). The Wisdom who called from the heights took on a body and rolled up his sleeves and worked the ordinary work of a carpenter's son. He rose while it was yet night and provided food for his household, fed five thousand, washed the feet, set the table in the upper room. He opened his hand to the poor. The teaching of kindness was on his tongue. And his works praise him in the gates of a city that crucified him and could not keep him in the ground. He is wisdom embodied, valor in a body, the fear of the LORD made flesh, the one in whom the whole book finally closes.

The book does not end with achievement. It ends with the fear of the LORD outlasting everything that decays, the charm that deceives, the beauty that fades, the strength that ages. One thing endures the dawn, and it is the same thing the book began with.

Charm is deceptive. Fear endures.
